content: Babies who are switched at birth are infants who are mistakenly or intentionally exchanged with another baby at the time of birth or shortly thereafter. This results in the babies being unknowingly raised by parents who are not their biological parents. While such occurrences are exceedingly rare in real life, there have been a few documented cases. However, the concept of babies being switched at birth is a recurring theme in fictional narratives. In literature, the idea of babies being switched at birth has been a popular plot device since the 18th century, particularly in American fiction. This trope is a hallmark of melodrama, often involving highly improbable scenarios. The theme has been used consistently over time. For instance, W.S. Gilbert incorporated this device in the Gilbert and Sullivan operas H.M.S. Pinafore and The Gondoliers, where babies of noble birth were switched with those of commoners. Similarly, Mark Twain employed this plot in The Tragedy of Pudd'nhead Wilson (1893), where a white baby and a black baby were switched at birth, leading to both children being raised as members of the opposite race. The theme of switched babies became especially prominent in made-for-TV movies during the 1970s and 1980s and has remained popular in the 1990s and 21st century. Examples include its use in the television series Veronica Mars (with the characters Cindy Mac Mackenzie and Madison Sinclair), Neighbours (with Bree Timmins and Anne Baxter), and The Young and the Restless (involving characters such as Cane Ashby and Phillip Chancellor III, as well as the children of Lauren Fenmore Baldwin and Sheila Carter). While this plot device is common in soap operas, it is not as prevalent as the theme of questionable paternity. According to Mumford, this is because the causes of questionable paternity are more varied and complex, offering richer material for storytelling. Questionable paternity can arise from scenarios such as a woman falsely attributing paternity to a man, unreported sexual assault, or secret love affairs. Additionally, it is easier for writers to retroactively introduce questions of paternity into a storyline, whereas introducing doubts about maternity is more challenging since it typically requires a specific event, such as a baby being switched at birth. The concept of switched babies is not limited to American fiction. For example, it appears in the French operetta The Little Michus. In real life, the likelihood of babies being switched at birth is extremely low. However, there have been a few notable cases that garnered media attention. One such case involved a girl in Wauchula, Florida, who was switched at birth due to a medical error. This incident was later dramatized in the made-for-TV movie Switched at Birth. Another case occurred in South Africa in 1989, where two women, Margaret Clinton-Parker and Sandra Dawkins, had their sons accidentally switched at birth. In 1995, they sued the government of Gauteng province for damages, and the High Court of South Africa awarded them compensation to cover medical expenses and future costs related to visiting their biological children. Despite learning of the switch, both families chose to continue raising the children they had been living with. In another case, on December 9, 2006, two newborn girls were switched at birth in a hospital in the Czech town of Třebíč. The error was not discovered until September 2007, when friends of one of the fathers joked that he did not resemble his daughter. A DNA test confirmed the switch, and after an investigation, the other family was located. As of October 11, 2007, the families were in contact and working on plans to exchange the children back. To prevent such errors, hospitals implement strict protocols, such as taking fingerprints, footprints, or palm prints of newborns.
